title: The Wisdom and Madness of Crowds
question: Why do independent groups of strangers sometimes estimate the truth more accurately than any expert among them—and why do the same groups sometimes spiral into shared delusion?
summary: Averaging many independent guesses can outperform any single expert, but the same aggregation mechanism, once independence breaks down, produces bubbles, panics, and mass delusion instead.
content:
In 1906, the statistician Francis Galton attended a livestock fair where 787 people guessed the weight of an ox in a competition. No individual guess was particularly accurate. But the median of all 787 guesses came within one pound of the ox's true weight—closer than the estimate of any single butcher or farmer in the crowd. Galton, who believed strongly in the superiority of trained experts over the untrained masses, was startled enough to publish the result. It became one of the founding observations behind what's now called the "wisdom of crowds": aggregate enough independent judgments and their errors tend to cancel out, leaving something more accurate than any individual contributor.

Why Averaging Works

The mechanism is mathematically simple. If each person's guess is the true value plus some random error, and those errors are independent and unbiased, averaging many guesses averages away the noise while preserving the signal. This is the same logic behind polling, ensemble methods in machine learning, and prediction markets. It works remarkably well for problems with a definite right answer—the weight of an ox, the number of jellybeans in a jar, the release date of a product—precisely because each guesser's error is idiosyncratic rather than shared.

Where the Wisdom Collapses

The word doing all the work in that mechanism is "independent." The moment people stop guessing independently and start guessing based on each other, the math changes entirely. If guesses at the fair had been announced aloud one by one, each new guesser would have anchored on what came before, and errors would have compounded instead of canceling. This is exactly what happens in financial bubbles, bank runs, and viral misinformation: instead of many independent estimates of value or truth, you get a cascade where each person's belief is shaped by watching others, and the crowd converges on a shared answer that may be wildly wrong. Charles Mackay described this a full sixty years before Galton's ox, cataloguing tulip mania, the South Sea Bubble, and witch-hunt panics under the title "Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds." The wisdom and the madness are not two different phenomena—they're the same aggregation mechanism running with and without independence.

The Same Machinery, Opposite Outputs

This is what makes the topic more than a curiosity: the conditions that produce wisdom (diversity of opinion, independence of judgment, decentralization, and some mechanism to aggregate individual views) are exactly the conditions that social media, social proof, and herding behavior tend to erode. A Twitter pile-on, a stock rally driven by momentum rather than fundamentals, or a run on a bank are all cases where visibility of others' choices destroys the independence that made crowd aggregation valuable in the first place. Recommendation algorithms that show people what's already popular can quietly convert a wisdom-generating crowd into a madness-generating one, because they make prior choices highly visible and easy to copy.

Designing for Wisdom, Not Madness

Prediction markets, blind peer review, and secret-ballot voting are all institutional attempts to preserve independence deliberately, because we've learned that simply gathering many people together is not sufficient—the structure of how they're allowed to influence each other determines whether you get Galton's ox or Mackay's tulip mania. This has real design implications for anything built on aggregated human judgment: a jury, a Wikipedia edit war, an online rating system, or a large language model trained on the collective text of the internet, which is itself, in a sense, one enormous aggregation of human judgments whose wisdom or madness depends on properties of the underlying data that aren't always visible from the outside.

perspectives.title: Statistics Perspective
perspectives.description: Averaging independent, unbiased estimates cancels random error while preserving signal, which is the mathematical core of why crowd aggregation can outperform individual experts.

perspectives.title: Behavioral Economics Perspective
perspectives.description: Herding, social proof, and information cascades break the independence assumption, turning the same aggregation mechanism into a driver of bubbles and panics rather than accuracy.

perspectives.title: Sociology Perspective
perspectives.description: Historical episodes of mass delusion—from tulip mania to witch panics—show that shared belief can spread through a population independent of any underlying truth, given the right social conditions.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Ensemble methods in machine learning deliberately engineer independence among models to replicate the wisdom-of-crowds effect, while recommendation systems risk destroying it by amplifying visible popularity.

openQuestions: Can a social platform be designed to preserve independence of judgment while still allowing people to see and learn from each other?
Do large language models trained on collective human text inherit crowd wisdom, crowd madness, or some unpredictable mixture of both?
How much visible social influence is enough to tip a wise crowd into a deluded one, and is there a measurable threshold?
Are there real-world domains where the 'madness' outcome is actually more accurate than the 'wisdom' outcome, inverting the usual story?
